Epic Games no longer plans to include Blueprints or Actor Gameplay Framework in Unreal Engine 6
Until recently Epic had maintained that both features would initially remain options in Unreal Engine with plans to wind down the features over time, but now Blueprints and the Actor Gameplay Framework have been dropped in favor of support for AI driven tools.

Image via Epic
Revising plans for the upcoming iteration of Unreal Engine, Epic has announced that it will not support Blueprints or Actor Gameplay Framework on Unreal Engine 6. Instead, the focus will be on Verse and Scene Graph, a proprietary code language and a hierarchical system that both lean heavily on AI for creation.
The announcement comes from
the Unreal Engine website in a post
titled "An update on Blueprints and the path to UE6." While Epic had announced in June that Blueprints and Actor Gameplay Framework
would be deprecated over time
, they would still exist in Unreal Engine 6 as an option. Now, Epic says, that is no longer the plan because of advances in AI.
"In June, we said Blueprints and Actors would coexist in UE6 Early Access and 6.0, so UE5 projects could upgrade incrementally while the new Scene Graph framework matures," the post reads. "However, with recent advances in AI capability, we expect AI to massively help with converting UE5 projects to UE6, if not make that process fully automatic. That also means we can deliver UE6 on time (or sooner!) while meeting its design goals: a new data model, a Verse-first architecture, modularity, and AI operability."
Related:
Devs can now utilize the high-end ambient occlusion technique seen in EVE: Frontier
This is undoubtedly a big blow to game studios that rely heavily on Blueprints. The tool has been utilized by games like the award-winning
Clair Obscur: Expedition 33
, which developer Sandfall states was
"95 percent built" with Blueprints
. Former Valve writer
Chet Faliszek points out on social media
that this move from Epic complicates cross-discipline efforts when working on a game and that his team will be staying on Unreal Engine 5. According to Faliszek, the current system allows for the ability to take charge of certain aspects of development, while the change to a prompt-based model removes it from their hands.
The changes to Unreal Engine 6 follow Epic announcing its focus on
an AI-first business model
, which many had thought would initially exclude Unreal Engine, or at least offer developers options regarding UE6's AI tools.. For now, though, developers who have come to rely on Unreal Engine features that don't depend on AI seemingly seem content to stay on Unreal Engine 5, which Epic appears to have no interest in changing.
